chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara’s pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma’s root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara’s ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva’s ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
Meditation on developing regret. With the Buddhas in the space in front, we can feel our reading Shantideva's words directly to us. We can contemplate as follows.

With my palms pressed together, I make request to those endowed with great compassion, the perfect Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas who abide throughout the ten directions. Since beginningless time in samsara, throughout this and all my previous lives, out of ignorance I have committed evil, ordered it to be committed, and overwhelmed by deceptive ignorance, rejoiced in its being committed by others. Seeing all these to be grave mistakes, from the depths of my heart I confess them to the holy beings.

Whatever harmful actions of body, speech or mind I have done under the influence of delusion towards the three precious jewels, my father and mother, my spiritual guide and others, all the extremely unbearable evil actions committed by me, an evil person, polluted by many faults. I confess before the deliverers, the enlightened beings, but I might die before I purify all my negativities. So please protect me so that I may surely and swiftly be freed from them, since the untrustworthy lord of death will not wait while I purify my evils.

Regardless of whether I am sick or not, this momentary life is unreliable. I shall have to leave everything and depart alone. But through failing to understand this, I have committed many kinds of evil action with respect to my friends and others.

And yet my friends will become nothing, and others will also become nothing. Even I shall become nothing. Likewise, everything will become nothing.

Just like an experience in a dream, everything I now enjoy will become a mere recollection, for what has passed cannot be seen again.

As we reflect on these points, especially focus on the fact that we have definitely created negative karma that has not been purified, and that unless this negative karma is purified, it will definitely, 100%, result in suffering and problems. Not only that, this negative karma is increasing, and it will not waste away on its own.

Just try to deeply internalize these truths, and when a powerful intention that wants to purify negative karma arises, you can hold that single-pointedly, deep in your heart. Before you get distracted, just return back to especially this main point — that we definitely have negative karma in our mental continuum, and it will definitely result in suffering and problems if it is not purified. 100% chance.

So therefore, we must purify now. If we develop this intention, which is virtuous regret, we can just hold this single-pointedly, without distraction.

Then we can look at the last week, specifically at our meditation break practice, and just ask ourselves: how did it go? Did we remember our break practice? Perhaps thinking about karma, or purification, or did we forget? If we remembered, why did we remember? And what can we learn from that? And if we forgot, why did we forget? And what can we learn from that?

Just check very gently, but honestly, and come to some conclusion about the break practice. Just hold whatever conclusion we've gained in our heart, and then in our own time, gradually arise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Grady
postMeditation.text: All right, here we are again.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Yippee! And let's do different verses today. Maybe we can start from 37, in Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life. And we can go to 48, perhaps. 37 to 48. Does anyone like to read that, please?

shantidevaReading.speaker: Anne K
shantidevaReading.text:
(37) Even during this brief life,
Many friends and others have passed away;
But the unbearable results of the evil I have committed for their sake
Still lie ahead of me.

(38) Thus, through failing to realize
That I shall suddenly die,
I have committed many evils
Out of ignorance, attachment and anger.

(39) Remaining still neither day nor night,
This life is continuously slipping away
And never increases in duration;
So why should death not come to one such as me?

(40) Even if, as I lie on my deathbed,
I am surrounded by friends and relatives,
I alone shall have to experience
The feeling of my life being severed.

(41) Of what help will my companions be
When I am seized by the messengers of the Lord of Death?
At that time, only merit will protect me,
But upon that I have not relied.

(42) O Protectors, oblivious to dangers such as these,
I, who am devoid of conscientiousness,
Have committed many negative actions
For the sake of this transient life.

(43) Terrified is the person
Who today is led away to a place where his limbs will be torn from his body.
With a dry mouth and sunken eyes,
His appearance is completely distorted.

(44) So what need is there to mention the terrible despair I shall experience
When, stricken by great panic,
I am seized by the physical apparitions
Of the terrifying messengers of the Lord of Death?

(45) Who can grant me real protection
From this great terror?
Petrified, with wide, bulging eyes,
I shall search for refuge in all directions.

(46) But seeing no refuge anywhere,
I shall become utterly dejected.
If I cannot find refuge there,
What shall I do at that time?

(47) Therefore, from today I go for refuge
To the Conqueror Buddhas who protect living beings,
Who seek to give refuge to all living beings,
And who, with their great strength, eradicate all fear.

(48) Likewise, I sincerely go for refuge
To the Dharma they have realized,
Which dispels the fears of samsara,
And to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne K
practiceReports.text:
I wanted to focus on the positive, which was, along with my purification buddy this week, I had a great experience of thinking about all the horrible things I've done in past lives. I really feel like there's a sense of lightness that comes after you purify. I'm like, ah, I didn't know that was in there, but now that it's not, I feel lighter. It's interesting.

But when you asked earlier how our meditation break practice went, I found myself getting really annoyed. And that's because — oh, I forgot to do the meditation break practice because I have one zillion other meditation break practices I'm supposed to be doing every day. And I feel like I failed. I failed at that one, which I know is a sign that I am not practicing properly. And you have advised me in the past, well, just combine them all into one.

But it's tricky, especially when there's a new practice every single day with this Lamrim thing we're all doing. Even if I could combine them all into one meditation break practice, the mental gymnastics required for that are just bonkers. I like things to be easy, simple. I like to do one thing at a time and really focus on it. And I feel like I didn't do well at my Lamrim stuff this week. I feel like I didn't focus enough on my meditation break practice for my class on Monday. And I completely failed at this meditation break practice with the purification. And that's not cool.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thank you. It's a good data report. And it's just helpful to look at that mind that feels agitated by all that. Because this investigation isn't designed to agitate us. It's designed to create clarity and focus and wisdom and peace and joy. So the agitation is the interesting part. It's not all the things — it's agitation. That's the delusion. That's the enemy. It's not having amazing Dharma practices to do all day. That's not the enemy. The enemy is the agitation.

And so I hope you can look at that. That's actually a huge help. Because when we have a somewhat ambitious Dharma practice going on, and it doesn't go according to plan, and then we feel agitated by it — that's a delusion functioning. And then what happens is either we don't want to look at what's going on in our practice because we don't enjoy the agitation of finding out, or we don't improve and refine because our response is just agitation. We're not actually being constructive.

So we need a way to look at when things don't go according to plan and be completely peaceful and delighted learning about it. That's the only way we're going to learn to be completely honest with our practice but then also learn what's really going on.

In general, though, the answer is: do it all. Do it all. It's not complicated. One of the Lamrim objects was literally karma — so that works well with this. One of them was refuge — that's purification practice. One of them was dangers of lower rebirth — perfect for thinking about karma and purification. It's all one. We don't need to feel overwhelmed by that. Maybe there's some headway that needs to be made in how to see things as one practice. But the main headway is in the agitation.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text:
First, I apologize for walking in late. I've been recovering from surgery, and my practice has been crappy or nonexistent. And I was beating myself up for that, feeling really bad. And then your words really helped. And so this morning, for the first time in a while, I sat down and did not the whole Heart Jewel, but most of it. And while I didn't have any great transformation, it felt peaceful.

I'm happy with peaceful. I'm very happy with peaceful right now. And when you get distracted by something happening in your life, especially surgery, it just shatters everything. It just takes it away. And I'm trying to learn from that experience because I had similar stuff — I had to have a lot of patience last year getting over something. And so I am trying to lock in the good stuff and slowly make my way back to what feels right for me.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, that's great, Dale. Thank you. It's the main lesson in those moments — when we get absolutely walloped by sickness, in your case surgery — it's just the incredible vulnerability that we have. As long as we identify with the suffering body and mind as us, we're all just incredibly vulnerable.

And Dale, you're right. Those times, the practice can go out the window. It can get really hard. And we want to use that. The way to not use it is to attack ourself. The way to use it is to go: whoa, I'm really vulnerable. As long as I keep thinking 'I' on the suffering body and mind, I'm totally at its mercy because it's just going to hop ship at some point or it's just going to crash at some point. And it's a little scary when that happens.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text: One more thing. In the continuum of having negative karma, where does a negative thought fall? Where does that come into it — that you don't act on but you have a negative thought? I know you said if you don't take action on that thought, the negative karma doesn't appear or arise. But I'm wondering what happens to the negative thought in terms of it affecting you.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah. So you're referring to the factors that create a complete action. There needs to be an intention. You need to have the right object. And then you need to have this sense of rejoicing or delight in whatever the action is.

So for example, hurtful speech: your intention needs to be negative — you really want to hurt someone. The object needs to be another person and needs to be truly hurtful speech. Then they need to have actually heard it and be hurt by it. And then we need to be kind of satisfied with it. It's only when those factors are all complete that it's called a complete action. And a complete action leads to all the different karmic effects — the ripened effect, environmental effect, effect similar to the cause, tendency similar to the cause.

It's still negative to have a negative thought. It's not like since they didn't do a complete action, it's all cool. It's just not a full action. The practical conclusion is: I want to make sure in all my actions that I'd never make the negative ones a complete action from this time forward. And then once I can start working on those, I can go further and even try to adjust the thoughts themselves.

practiceReports.speaker: Sumit
practiceReports.text:
My data is in response to the teaching skills class from last week. And out of that, I just sort of doubled down. You talked about the book a lot. So I doubled down on reading from the book and quotes and stuff like that. And it was really great. I got a lot of really positive feedback from people who I don't think normally do. And they even said, I don't really know why. They couldn't even identify why, but they found it to be a great class.

And I felt very inspired by that. And I decided I'm going to read and kind of build up to the HYT this summer. I'm rereading New Essence of Vajrayana. And just the beginning — really basic stuff, like here's what should be on your shrine — but I'm feeling really like, oh yeah, that's awesome.

The point being, just the power of Geshe-la's words. It's just incredible. Way back when, Gen-la Dekyong was here and said, you can imagine that Geshe-la is talking to us through the words. Imputing that power upon the words of the books is just really, really fruitful.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thank you, Sumit. It's beautiful. It's funny — I did end up talking to someone who was at the Thursday Bed-Stuy class, and they said, 'Sumit gave this amazing teaching on overcoming self-cherishing.' They just said it to me kind of off the cuff. They were really raving about it.

The point of the teaching skills class is basically that we want to make sure that the teachings are grounded in the Dharma — in specifically the words themselves. There's an incredible depth and breadth to them. And there's a blessing to them, because we're passing on lineage.

One thing I found, similar to what you're saying, Sumit, is that because when I'm trying to put things in my own words, it's belabored and random sometimes and convoluted. But the act of reading chunks of the text — it just makes the class actually dense with tons of rich stuff. It's impossible in your own words to teach like that.

Last thing on this: I had the same experience yesterday. In the day course I used a lot of the texts, a lot of the words. And a woman who's been coming on and off for a couple of years said to me the exact same thing. She said, 'That class was really different and special. What did you do?' And I just said, 'I think you just got a blessing of the oral lineage.' She said, 'Ah, okay, a blessing. Sounds good.' Same kind of feedback.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
Just before my little piece, I wanted to thank Sumit for bringing that up, because it reminded me when Gen-la Dekyong said that when we're reading the books, to imagine that Geshe-la is reading them to us. And I've forgotten to do that. I want to bring that back.

My data is sort of a follow-up to what Anne was saying, because I had a similar but very different experience with the daily Lamrim practice. That was the meditation break that I was focusing on each day, combined with an ongoing practice of looking at how purely I'm cherishing other people — developing, working on developing, looking at my self-cherishing mind and the mind that cherishes other people.

So I was feeling like I was doing really well with my practice, and I don't often feel that way. I had a good week. And then when you asked, 'How did your meditation break practice go?' — I was like, what was the meditation break practice for this class? And it sort of cut me off. This pride that I had in my practice was, hold on a second, TTP.

I have a tendency to close the book on Sunday and not really remember. And I'll get the email from Sumit — oh yeah, that's what we're supposed to be doing. So this was really great, because I had a good week practicing, but this was a reminder not to be too prideful in that and think that that's really good enough, because it's not.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thanks, Fran. It's interesting — just that question riled everyone up into a little tizzy. That means we're going to keep asking it over and over again. At least for two years. Someone mark the date. We'll put it on the Google Calendar — two years from today we can stop asking that question at the beginning of class.

It is good, because this is related very closely to what we're about to do — looking at regret and guilt and shame and things like this. It's all tied up in one little lovely knot. In modern times, this stuff is completely confused. This is actually really helpful, hearing some of these thoughts.

practiceReports.speaker: Kristin
practiceReports.text:
I read in on the WhatsApp and appreciated your help there, because part of my question — for anybody who didn't see that — was that it feels like purifying all of the negativities from countless lives is so vast. Then when getting to the promise piece, it seems hard to choose something specific to promise not to. It was helpful that you steered me toward focusing on practicing effort in the day as opposed to just practicing Dharma.

The second part of my question was about this idea of, okay, I've successfully purified all negativity from countless lives, which is great, but then tomorrow, did I do it again? I mean, in a day, despite my best effort, I am accumulating a lot of negative karma. That's the only part that feels kind of like, hmm, what?

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah. So when we do a purification practice, at the end we imagine that Vajrasattva or whoever melts into light, dissolves into us, and we become completely pure. We think, I've completely purified all my negativity, and I'm experiencing a pure land. Pure mind, pure world.

And then we try to hold that for as many seconds or milliseconds as possible, both in the meditation and then in the meditation break. For as long as we can hold that, it's great. We're completely purified from that point of view. If we can then hold it to the next day, then we don't need to purify again the next day.

But for most of us, our mind reverts very quickly out of that correct belief — 'I'm completely purified' — into seeing an ordinary world, having ordinary minds, grasping an ordinary self. And if that's the case, then we need to do it again the next day.

It's similar to thinking 'I'm Heruka' or 'I'm Vajrayogini.' We can think that even before we are Heruka or Vajrayogini because it's a correct belief on the valid base of imputation. It doesn't mean we are literally Heruka or Vajrayogini yet because we still have the karma to appear in an impure world. The belief is correct. It's coming from wisdom. It's on a valid base of imputation. But unless we're never going to think otherwise ever again, we're not actually Heruka or Vajrayogini yet. It's just a correct belief. And so when the belief drops again — okay, now we have to go back to purifying.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text:
So this is my data. I started the week saying that I was a rotten log and I was going to open up my chest and have all the worms come out and just sunbathe in that thought. And the week was great. I did purification practice. I did Vajrayogini. I was purifying hell realm by hell realm, trotting along, doing okay. And life was pretty happy.

And on Friday — well, actually it was Wednesday — I got this message from my boss. She said, can you come to my office because we have this project. I said, okay, how about Friday? So I went on Friday to meet with her. I have a very good relationship with her. So I just bumbled in, talking about my stuff. And she was like — I noticed something was off. I was intuiting like something's off.

And after a while, she said, 'I need to talk to you. At work, I'm known as Marianne, by the way. She says, I need to talk to you, Marianne, about something.' And her tone — my heart just fell. 'I need to talk to you about your time.' In my department, you have to be on time. We punch in and punch out. And I've been in the hospital for a long, long time and I've had a really good reputation. But I have been running late. And I have this attitude like, oh, I've been in the hospital for so long, it doesn't really matter. I'm senior. That attitude.

And she said, 'Your colleagues have noticed.' And I was so embarrassed. I was mortified. And defensive. Like, oh my God, I can't believe my peers are talking about me behind my back.

But it was like, oh, rotten log. Buddha always delivers. He always delivers. So I said, Erin, I'm sorry. You're right. I'm going to correct this. And I felt accountable and responsible. She's right. I don't have any defense. And I left feeling kind of horrible icky. But I said to myself, you know what, Mimi? Just get up early. Get to work early. And don't be mad at your colleagues. It's a gift from them. They're helping you. And just look at it as part of your confession and your purification and just do it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thank you. These kind of things are very useful. Especially where it's somewhere that kind of hurts a little bit. And for each one of us, we have our own little things that hurt when they happen.

A karma ripening like this is just a great opportunity — just to take one for the team and not think it's my rat co-worker's fault, or justifying or whatever. Just think, yeah, this is my karma, 100%. And I've got to own this. And when it hurts and we do that, that's where it's really powerful. If it doesn't really hurt, it's not that powerful. But if it hurts and we can really own that, it's like a real spiritual realization in that moment.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Page 88, Meaningful to Behold. Without the strong sense of regret so powerfully illustrated by Shantideva above, we'll be unable to purify our non-virtue. Yet generally, we do not even feel slightly regretful of our past non-virtuous actions. Why? Because we do not fully realize that the fruits of these actions will be nothing but suffering. As long as we remain ignorant of the causal relationship between deluded non-virtuous actions and the resulting experiences of misery, we will neither abandon nor regret our misguided way of life. We'll not only be unable to purify the effects of past negativities, but we'll continue to create the causes for even more suffering in the future.

We can cultivate an attitude of regret only when we recognize the connection between the harm we create and the harm we receive. It's nice just to think of those as two little points. And right now, harm we create, harm we receive — these two points usually aren't linked with a line between them. For most people, the relationship is not direct. A big part of this whole thing is just rewiring those two points to each other. It's actually kind of simple. And if we just do that over and over and make that wire completely linked, then the rest of the practice will follow. We'll definitely be able to have a powerful purification practice.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 355–356: Wiring harm we create to harm we receive
teaching.text:
Part of our mind is trying to figure this out. We don't particularly think about harm we create — where that goes. But we usually are trying to figure out harm we receive. We're making connections. Eat this food, feel awful. Be around that mean bully person, feel like I receive harm. Too hot, too cold, didn't get enough sleep. We're making these connections in our mind, trying to wire: why am I receiving harm?

Even a baby is doing this. They do things and get hurt, and they start to wire something. They almost have very few conceptual ideas yet, but they can figure it out.

When we get into Buddhism, Buddha is offering a slightly different idea. He's saying, all those things maybe are related in some way, but they're not the actual link. They're just conditions. The harm we receive is always linked to the karma that we've created.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 356–357: Regret vs. guilt, the match analogy
teaching.text:
However, it is important not to misunderstand what it means to regret our unskillful actions. We should not view the suffering we experience as an externally applied punishment for our sins. Nor is it necessary to feel guilty, thinking we have offended some authority or force that is prepared to take revenge upon us. True regret is not concerned with such extraneous attitudes.

These kind of feelings are habitual for a lot of people. They're not innate, but they are habitual. Often they can be reinforced through various people in power in our life. Even the way we're taught as a kid. One of the ways maybe our parents try to teach us is by punishing us when we do the wrong thing. They're trying to be like a karmic enforcer for us, which has varying degrees of effects. And many other aspects of life are like this — we have laws and police and authority figures and bosses that call us in for being late every day. So it's very easy to internalize that.

The difference between a proper and exaggerated attitude can be illustrated as follows. A boy's parents, recognizing the dangers of fire, have prohibited him from playing with matches. He does so anyway and burns his finger. The proper, most beneficial response would be for the child to regret his carelessness and learn from his painful experience to avoid similar dangers in the future. An exaggerated response would be for the child to think that the match deliberately punished him for disobeying his parents. Such a superstitious reaction only confuses the situation and introduces extraneous considerations such as guilt that might in fact reduce rather than increase his ability to deal with future dangerous situations intelligently.

Can someone explain why guilt would actually reduce the ability to deal with dangerous situations?

teaching.speaker: Marianne (Mary Ann)
teaching.text: Because if he was just thinking linearly — okay, match, burn, done, I won't do that again — but the guilt makes it seem like he gets involved in thinking too much about himself. Like, oh, what was I thinking? Why did I do it? It kind of internalizes what should just be pretty external.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: When you experience guilt, you experience a lot of self-grasping. Basically, I am a bad person. I'm a naughty person. And you're grasping at that — that's who I am. And maybe I can cover it up, but the truth is I am a bad person. It's like a judgment — when you go to court and they say, you are a murderer. That's very problematic because then you don't relate to it as something that you can remove from yourself.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, so in a mind of guilt, there's actually grasping at some identity of being a bad person, which would then make you less able to deal with future dangerous situations — because you're thinking, I, who am a bad person, I'm going to try to avoid these bad actions. It's quite contradictory.

teaching.speaker: Dale
teaching.text: Isn't that reinforcing a really bad delusion? And that's what he would fall back on in the future — oh, I'm a really bad person, so that's why this is happening to me. And it repeats the cycle.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: I was thinking that introducing the external authority complicates matters. As long as you keep that authority happy, then you can kind of do whatever you want, and it becomes more about appeasing that authority. Or if the authority is not happy with you, then it doesn't really matter what you do. It just weakens the link between your actions and harm, and introduces this extra thing that doesn't help.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, that's an important part. It reduces the ability to deal with future dangerous situations intelligently. Because it's very easy to internalize the lesson as: obey my parent and don't get caught making a mistake. Instead of: touch fire, get burned, be hurt. Those are completely different lessons. One is about appeasing the authority, or at least just not getting caught. The other is simple cause and effect.

This is why for a lot of people, living within the law of karma can be tricky. Because there's no one watching. And we know how to behave when there's a watcher. But there was never a watcher. It's just been karma the whole time.

teaching.speaker: Marianne (Mary Ann)
teaching.text: With karma, I just feel like it implies a moral universe. And that's the kind of thing where my mind goes, and I often just tell myself, stop, because it's a hidden object. You're not going to understand it really very well yet. I just feel like if it's a moral universe, I don't get the mechanics. So then I think, oh, it's energetic. But I kind of get stuck on how it works. I know there's no person meting out judgment, but how come a harm a thousand years ago that you did would make you experience it? I do believe in karma. I sometimes wonder, does that imply a moral universe? It's just the materialism — the Western outlook that the only real thing is the material world.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Practical approach to understanding karma mechanics
teaching.text:
Yeah, trying to figure out the mechanics has some degree of help, as long as there's a practical intention behind it. We don't want to try to figure it out just for arbitrary intellectual stimulation. If there's a practical intention — thinking, what's the practical problem I'm trying to solve in my day-to-day practice? And there are some practical problems that improving our understanding of karma mechanics would help with.

Your thread about the bias that comes from believing in a material universe is an interesting one to pull on. It's like, how's that bias clouding the analysis? Sometimes the best way forward is to remove the cloud first. It's like a telescope covered in muck and dirt. You could squint really hard and try to improve the telescope to see through the muck. Or you could just clean the muck off the lens — that would get you a lot further, a lot more quickly.

So sometimes with a Dharma topic, especially something subtle, it's worth our time to identify the biases that are clouding our analysis, identify them, and uproot them first.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraph 358 + How to Understand the Mind on three types of regret
teaching.text:
So guilt. How much do we identify with being guilty? How much does guilt play a role in our life and our practice?

Returning now to the proper application of the opponent powers, we should try to cultivate an attitude of regret towards our unskillful, non-virtuous actions that is based not upon guilt, but rather upon a clear understanding that harmful causes bring harmful results.

From How to Understand the Mind, the four changeable mental factors section on regret. Regret is one of the changeable mental factors, which means it can be positive, negative, or neutral. It depends on how you approach it.

Definition of regret: a mental factor that feels remorse for actions done in the past. There are three types. Virtuous regret: developed by recognizing the faults and disadvantages of non-virtuous actions. Those who have not heard teachings on karma will find it difficult to develop sincere regret and therefore will not be able to purify their negative actions. One of the greatest gifts of Dharma is that it teaches us how to purify our past non-virtues.

We need to develop regret for past negative actions before their effects have ripened. There is no point in feeling regret for non-virtuous actions whose effects have already ripened because it is too late to do anything about them. Once something has already ripened, that's more just about learning from it. Regret is about wanting to purify something that hasn't ripened yet. Guilt is a bit like just living in the past — oh, why did I do that? Regret is about action — I have negative karma in my mind that hasn't ripened yet. I want to uproot it before it does occur.

Feeling regret for previously created virtuous actions is non-virtuous regret. Some practitioners may develop this by regretting having taken vows or by becoming unhappy about having commitments or by regretting having made an offering. Like, oh, I regret joining TTP. I could have had my Sundays free and sat at the park and gotten sunburn and skin cancer. We should never develop such regrets. We don't want to blame the virtuous things we're doing for our unhappiness. That's miswiring what's going on.

Neutral regret is very common. If we eat unhealthy food and feel ill, we regret having eaten it. Even though neutral regret is not non-virtuous, it's generally better to avoid it because it can lead to unhappiness and serves no useful function. There's a saying in Tibetan: the wise person checks beforehand, the fool feels regret afterwards.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: I have a question about not purifying karma that's already ripened. Because the karma is continually ripening every moment. Being born blind, or I received a cancer diagnosis — that's my karma for having done whatever. I can't change that moment, but I think I can still purify the ongoing karma that's creating this ongoing issue. Is that correct?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, that's correct. A lot of times when we're feeling guilty and having non-virtuous regret or these negative mindsets, it's because we're living in the past and thinking this shouldn't have happened. You can't reverse it from having happened through purification. We all sort of know that, but if we check our mind, there's a habit to do that. Why did I do that? I should have never done that. Those thoughts are incredibly pointless and completely extraneous. They don't add to anything. They don't make us learn or change. They just make us live in the past constantly and obsessively.

But yeah, if there's something that has continual negative karma ripening to maintain, we can definitely purify that before it ripens.

So just to simplify into two points. One, we want to improve this connection: harmful actions, harmful results. But we want to do that without inducing extraneous feelings like guilt. We want to turn that into regret — the wish to purify. Harmful actions, harmful results, therefore I need to purify. Not harmful actions, harmful results, therefore I'm a big-time loser.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text: Let's take a break now. We'll come back at 6:15 or so. Bed-Stuy public talk, 7 to 8:15, this Thursday. Phone-free summer, Saturday. And Kadam Morton's coming to visit on the 28th — whatever that Saturday is. Teaching on the union of karma and emptiness, the Middle Way. We gave him a real doozy. Two sessions. It should be a great day. I'm looking forward to it and hope you can come. It'd be nice for us to show up in rows and numbers to support him being here and making the trip.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: Let's dedicate. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.
chantedPrayers.note: KK introduced the Liberating Prayer with a 'sandbox mind' teaching — imagining blowing all the little grooves and shortcuts clean, hearing the prayer as if for the first time.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Opening: the sandbox mind — hearing prayers fresh
teaching.text:
With the Liberating Prayer, or any of our practices in prayers, sometimes just trying to wipe the slate clean on what I already know about it is very useful. I imagine that my mind is like a little sandbox, and all the little grooves I've made in it are like little lines in the sandbox. Those are my little shortcuts about life. All I do is imagine going like this, just blowing it all clean. Wiping all those little shortcuts that my mind's made about the world and about life. It's just like restarting new connections.

When we do things a lot, our mind creates shortcuts. The shortcuts are what we relate to. We don't relate to the thing itself. It's like, oh, annoying person — we create a shortcut. We stop relating to them as a three-dimensional person. We stop being open-minded. When we relate to enough shortcuts, our mind becomes very rigid, stuck in our ways. Everything becomes a bit boring.

With the prayers, this can happen. So let's try to do this with the Liberating Prayer right now. Just try to hear it completely fresh, like you've never heard it before. Really hear it. There's a whole path in there of sutra and tantra. There's a lot to explore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraph 359–361: Seeds, imprints, and karmic mechanics
teaching.text:
So we can continue on purification. Page 89. How is it that harmful results follow from harmful actions? It is through the force of an imprint placed on our mind that the potential to experience future suffering comes about. For example, a person who commits murder plants a very strong negative impression on his or her own mind, and that impression, or seed, carries with it the potential to place that mind in a state of extreme misery. Unless the impression of that non-virtuous action is purified, this latent seed will remain in the mind, its power dormant but unimpaired. When the appropriate circumstances are eventually met, the potential power of this impression will be activated and the seed will ripen as an experience of intense suffering — for instance, as a rebirth in a karmically created realm of hellish misery.

The situation is analogous to that of an arid piece of ground into which seeds were planted a long time ago. As long as these seeds are not somehow destroyed, they will retain their potential to grow. Should the ground be watered sufficiently, these long-forgotten seeds will suddenly sprout forth. In a similar fashion, our karmic actions plant their seeds in the field of our consciousness. And when we encounter the proper conditions, these seeds will sprout and bear their karmic fruit.

By performing and neglecting to purify negative, harmful actions, we place upon our mind countless seeds of similarly negative potential energy. The fruition of such seeds is not limited to the experience of a lower rebirth. As a result of causing harm to others in a previous life, we may find that this life is filled with much sickness. Also, the mental suffering and unhappiness of the present can be the result of our having disturbed others in the past. Poverty is the karmic result of miserliness, and having a very disfigured or ugly body is a result of anger. Furthermore, we need not wait until a future life to experience the result of non-virtue committed now. We have all experienced how anger and greed can bring us discomfort and unhappiness almost immediately.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Modern Buddhism: simplifying karma. Acknowledging what we already have.
teaching.text:
From Modern Buddhism, Geshe-la says: from virtuous actions comes happiness, from non-virtuous actions comes suffering. If we believe in this, we believe in karma.

It's really nice just to ponder that one truth. And I think we all agree and believe in that to some degree. We just think, yeah, being a loving, good person, that's going to make me happier. Being a mean, greedy, miserable person, that's going to give me a worse life.

So whenever we're studying a topic, we need to acknowledge what we already have. We don't want to focus on moving forward thinking we don't have anything. We want to think: I'm moving it forward, acknowledging that I already have a lot. I already live within the law of karma to some degree. We probably don't just lie, cheat, and steal willy-nilly, even though we might not think we'll ever get caught. So why is that? It's that we already have this understanding.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Great Treasury of Merit on confession; purifying ordinary appearances
teaching.text:
There's a nice section in Great Treasury of Merit on confession. It's a nice thing to have in our back pocket because it explicitly goes through all the stages of the path, Sutra and Tantra. It goes through all the seven limbs, additional teachings on reliance on the spiritual guide, all the different Lojong teachings. And each page is pretty much completely unique to this book.

Geshe-la says here: 'In the presence of the Great Compassionate Ones, I confess with a mind of great regret all the non-virtues and negative actions that since beginningless time I have done, ordered to be done, or rejoiced in, and I promise that from now on I shall not commit them again.'

If we want to overcome problems and experience happiness, and if we want to meet with success in our spiritual practices, we must purify the negativity in our mental continuum. If we do not purify our negative karma, it will be very difficult for pure minds, such as bodhichitta and wisdom-realizing emptiness, to arise. A mind filled with non-virtuous imprints cannot give rise to pure states of mind, because the cause is impure. If the mind itself is impure, the objects that appear to it will also be impure. Without purifying the mind, the pure appearances of generation stage and completion stage will be unattainable.

So when we go about our day and see ordinary appearances — an inherently existent person, a suffering living being, non-Buddha — that is actually negative karma ripening. It's the effect of our ordinary appearances and conceptions. This is very helpful: I have to purify that too.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Karmic inheritance: why virtue is hard and non-virtue is easy
teaching.text:
We've been accumulating negative actions since beginningless time, and the burden of this negativity weighs heavily upon us. We can know that we've created a great deal of negativity simply by examining our experiences in this life. For example, we can train in spiritual practices for a long time and accomplish almost no results. Yet we can commit negative actions spontaneously, without any effort. Why? Because we've inherited from our previous lives a strong familiarity with non-virtue.

This is a reason people get discouraged. They're like, I'm trying to practice, and it's hard to focus, hard to be loving, hard to be patient. But the teaching here is no — just use that as proof of the karmic inheritance that needs to get purified. Oh, why is it easy to get angry and annoyed and attached, but hard to be contented and have renunciation? That's just showing me there's this huge burden of negativity weighing down upon us. Invisible, but dragging us down. We can use those moments as a little fire, a little encouragement: I've got to purify.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB: 'Why did it happen to me?' — conditions vs. causes, tomato/red car analogy
teaching.text:
Often when we experience suffering or misfortune, we look outside ourself for the cause. We may suffer from bad headaches and conclude that they're caused by eating sugar. But while it may be true that we develop headaches whenever we eat sugar, the question we need to ask is: why does this happen to me and not to others? If eating sugar were the main cause of headaches, everyone who ate sugar would suffer from headaches.

Similarly, if someone attacks us or steals something from us, we think it is the other person causing the harm, and that we are innocent victims. But once again, we need to think: why did he attack me and not someone else? The reason is we had created the cause and others had not. In reality, it was our negative karma ripening that caused the other person to attack us. From their side, they had no choice.

The question to ponder is: why did it happen to me, but not to others? People come up with different answers — genetics, something you said. But the more we probe, they're not satisfying answers.

The image I find useful: you have a garden, a tomato plant ripens. There's a red car outside. Tomato plant, red car — you go, huh, coincidence? Next season, tomato plants come again, red car. Oh yeah, I'm figuring something out. But it's just that your neighbor has a red car. This is what we're doing — our mind's trying to find patterns, seeing correlates. But the tomato plant is really caused by the tomato seed. It's not the red car. It's not even the soil. It's really the seed. And karma is the seed.

All the other little analyses, except for karma being the answer, are also superstitious.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraph 362: Wrong views as heaviest non-virtue; teaching Dharma skillfully
teaching.text:
Non-virtuous actions, such as theft, divisive speech, and malice, are committed with other beings serving as their intended objects or victims. There are certain mental actions, however, which are not directed outwardly, but instead affect the perpetrator directly. Such mental actions fall into the group known as holding wrong views and constitute the heaviest and most damaging of all unskillful actions.

One possible effect arising from such seeds is an experience of great difficulty when later trying to study or meditate on the Dharma. This is why we can't push someone into trying to understand the Dharma. We can't pressure someone into understanding it. If they don't understand it, it's largely because of the negative karma arising in their mind.

So how do you help them? Show a good example. Be kind and loving. Teach things clearly. But we can't control their journey. If it's coming from their negative karma of holding wrong views, just pushing it on someone isn't going to go anywhere.

I'm sharing this because sometimes when we're trying to teach the Dharma, it's a little bit like trying to sell it to people. And that's not exactly the right approach. We're trying to offer it very skillfully. But we're not trying to sell it or push it into them. They have their own journey. If we think about this when we teach Dharma, it helps us relax quite a bit.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: Everything you said, it all rings true. But sticking to the practical effects — if I were ever to tell a principal there's something wrong with the kid, absolutely not. That's never accepted. And I happily ascribe to that view teaching kids and teaching adults. We talk about pure view. But I wonder if it's a helpful view. I wonder if it's helpful for you.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
That's a really good question. Is it practically helpful to think like that? We always need to consider this with any teaching. Is there a practically helpful case where I'd want to use that view? And is there a way to unskillfully apply it in a way that might be destructive?

With this kind of teaching, there's definitely an unskillful application, which is sort of an excuse for laziness. Like, yes, I'm not trying, and I'm winging every teaching, and I'm not that nice, and no one's coming — and the only thing I can come up with is it must be their karma from holding wrong views. That's so unskillful. It's a coping mechanism trying to abdicate responsibility for the bad job we're doing.

But the place where it's really practically useful is: if our approach is somehow salesy or coercive or pushy, or we're trying to work with an arid piece of ground and getting distracted from ripe, fertile soil all around us. That's the case I'm talking about. But definitely not as an excuse.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: We say, karma for ourself, compassion for others. And I wonder — I take that as a tentpole. I don't think about your karma to other people. I don't know your karma. And that's been a guiding principle for me.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
It's so interesting. I really wonder where that phrase came from. I think it came from somewhere in Vajradhara Center. Until I came here, I'd never heard anyone say that. And since I've been here, I've heard it from many of the people in the sangha. It's a little saying that has germinated here.

Because there are teachings where we do explicitly think about karma for others. We think about their negative karma and how it causes them problems, and it's actually a reason to develop compassion for people — because they're trapped in the iron net of self-grasping, bound by the iron chains of karma, the pitch-black darkness of ignorance. We think about the fact that they're actually bound by their karma as a way to develop compassion.

The intention behind the saying might be: don't use Dharma to judge someone. Or don't use Dharma to close your heart off. We definitely want to use karma for others, but not in a judgmental way. The practice from Geshe Chekawa: do not turn a god into a demon. We can misapply any teaching for an unskillful result.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: I always took that to mean not to say to somebody who doesn't necessarily understand, 'Oh, that's your karma.' You should treat them with compassion rather than trying to convince them that it's their karma when they don't have that understanding. Apply it to yourself because we have a certain understanding, but not force it onto somebody else who may not understand it.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah. My rule of thumb for that is just: don't be an idiot. Going around to someone who's suffering, who has no idea of karma, going, 'Ha ha, it's your karma' — we've just lost the plot completely. We're so unskillful. If they're a Dharma practitioner and they're open and they trust our point of view, we can say that. But we need to be skillful. We have to be thoughtful about how our speech affects other people.

We should definitely think about other people's karma. But we should also be skillful in what we say and what we teach.

Okay, let's keep our regret going over this week ahead and wish to purify. Let's try to deepen the understanding. Move it forward in some practical and beneficial way, each one of us.

pairedDiscussion.note: Paired discussion removed. KK assigned geographical pairs: Mimi and Dale, Anne P and Sumit, Marianne (Mary Ann) and Anne K. David absent in person. Audio garbled in both Whale and Dolphin.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Yeah, let's go practice some Dharma, valiantly into the world. Okay, let's just dedicate. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any other personal prayers or dedications. Okay, thank you. Thanks, everyone. See you later.
